name: Colin Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior developer on accessible-route mapping software at a tech company, after years directing traffic and a two-year college diploma. I use AI every day for code examples, but a senior checks my changes and I walk a crossing before trusting its map. Mae, my partner, restores furniture, our children are grown, and my traffic knowledge helped me earn higher developer pay; we rent with thirteen months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the route-mapping team that a little AI help can draft a test faster, but a kerb ramp still has to be where the map says it is. I use AI every day for code examples and check the route against street photographs and my own walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58 and still a junior developer after a two-year college diploma, but my years directing traffic helped me get higher pay on this mapping project. Mae restores furniture, our grown children live elsewhere, and we rent with thirteen months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking one mapped crossing on foot each Friday with the senior developer’s review of my code. We would save 200 monthly while both wages hold and repair the balcony door before considering a new sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our own income and work. A ramp drawn on a map cannot carry a wheelchair over a high kerb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you spot on a walk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One route marked a smooth crossing, but the kerb had a sharp lip. I photographed the gap and corrected the test before an event venue used the map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why are you junior after traffic work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I learned code later than most of the team. I know the streets, but the senior developer still shows me how to make a change safely.

say: I want **mapped crossings** checked on foot.
I use **AI daily** for code examples, then verify the street.
think: I have **thirteen months saved** from higher developer pay and Mae’s furniture work.
I see **rent covered** even when furniture-restoration orders vary between months.
do: **Check one crossing** on foot weekly with senior code review.
**Save 200 monthly** while both wages hold; repair balcony door before buying sofa.
S0.quote: A ramp drawn on a map cannot carry a wheelchair over a high kerb.
fieldNote: His **traffic experience** explains high pay alongside junior coding skill.
Daily AI drafts are **existing practice**; street evidence and senior review still decide a route.

steps.text: Check one mapped crossing on foot weekly with senior code review
Save 200 monthly while both household wages continue
Repair balcony door before buying a new sofa

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking planning, checking and coding could build many of our route tests. I would want a person who uses the crossing to say whether the map works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior test-writing hours could shrink, though the project still needs people on the street. Thirteen months saved gives us room to look locally, but I would miss a full wage if the junior queue vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the lead for approved paid time to pilot a new AI route-checking tool on archived maps, with an accessibility user’s consent to review its errors. If approved, I’d bring one verified correction to the team weekly; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local mapping-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours but willing to test a tool carefully. A faster map is only useful when someone can travel the route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the correction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The accessibility user would check the route description, and my lead would approve the code. I would not put a live route change out on an AI suggestion alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay someone for that feedback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The project would need to fund the user’s time, with their consent and my manager’s approval. I would not ask for free accessibility advice as a shortcut.

say: I want **accessibility users paid** to check route changes.
I want **archived maps tested** before AI touches live routes.
think: I could lose **junior testing hours** despite knowing the streets.
I have **thirteen months saved**, but a lost wage still matters.
do: **Pilot AI route checks** weekly only with manager-approved paid time, funded user feedback and consent.
**Search paid mapping software** if hours fall and local vacancies cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious but active** about reduced junior hours.
S1.quote: A faster map is only useful when someone can travel the route.
fieldNote: His **new AI pilot** needs paid time and funded consent-based user review, beyond everyday AI examples.
The **local job search** starts only if his hours shrink and a bill-covering vacancy exists.

steps.text: Pilot archived AI route checks weekly only with approved paid time and funded consenting user review
Search paid local mapping-software vacancies if hours fall and wages cover rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write mapping code and evaluate street photographs cheaper than our team. Robots walking and measuring physical crossings may arrive about 2031, after our screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior developer role could end. Thirteen months saved and plenty of nearby tech firms give me search time, but Mae’s furniture work alone would not replace my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d postpone the sofa purchase and ask for written notice of developer cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local pedestrian-route survey vacancies only if they exist, the walking load fits my health and wages cover rent and bills; I would not buy surveying equipment on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing my own wage, even though I can plan. A map with no job behind it will not pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you return to directing traffic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a paid local opening exists and I can meet its current safety requirements. I would not call my old experience a guaranteed shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own lives, and Mae and I have saved so that we can search for paid work without using their wages.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach mapping code first.
I expect **crossing robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **junior developer wage** could end.
I know **thirteen months saved** is search time, not income.
do: **Postpone sofa purchase** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for route surveying** after 2028 loss only if local vacancies fit health and cover rent and bills.
S2.quote: A map with no job behind it will not pay the rent.
fieldNote: His **field-work option** requires a real paid local vacancy, safe walking load and bill-covering wage.
He protects **thirteen months saved** instead of buying equipment for speculative work.

steps.text: Postpone buying a new sofa when developer cuts threaten
Apply for paid local route-survey vacancies if displaced after 2028, health permits and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives a few years to test which crossings need on-foot measurement. Robots measuring the street may follow around 2034, after mapping code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn to run a proper route-access check with users while the developer wage lasts, although robots and AGI may later do much of it. I would not claim to know what a wheelchair user needs from my own walk alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the project lead for a paid monthly route audit with one consenting wheelchair user whose time the project funds. If approved, I’d measure a crossing and compare it with our map under the senior surveyor’s supervision; we would save 180 monthly while both wages hold, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local access-survey vacancies only if qualified, safe for my health and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about coding work, but learning from a real route user would make the preparation worthwhile. A photograph cannot show how a wheelchair wheel catches on a high kerb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record the kerb height, surface slope and distance to the next safe crossing. The user would tell me which part actually blocks the trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the project will not pay the user?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not run the audit as free consultation. I would keep coding and ask again when there is a funded project slot.

say: I want **paid user-led audits** before AGI reaches route code in 2031.
I expect **street robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I could learn **access surveying** while earning my current wage.
I need **user evidence**, not my own walking assumptions.
do: **Learn monthly route audit** only with approved paid time, funded consenting user and senior surveyor supervision.
**Apply for access-survey vacancies** after 2031 loss only if qualified, health-safe paid local work covers bills.
feel: **Anxious but engaged** with funded user-led practice.
S3.quote: A photograph cannot show how a wheelchair wheel catches on a high kerb.
fieldNote: He learns **specific kerb measurements** with paid user input, consent and senior supervision.
A later **survey job** remains contingent on qualification, safe walking and bill-covering local pay.

steps.text: Learn monthly access audit only with approved paid time, funded consenting user and senior supervision
Save 180 monthly while both household wages continue
Apply for qualified paid local access-survey vacancies if displaced after 2031, health-safe and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2036 gives us ten years to improve route records and try small paid street-mapping projects. Robots walking physical routes may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not checked a retirement amount and will not build a plan from one. Thirteen months saved lets me risk a small side project, but only if the rent reserve stays above ten months and a client actually pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing route code and save 190 monthly while both wages hold. If my employer permits outside work, a venue signs a paid order and project costs stay below 150 while ten months of expenses remain untouched, I’d map one accessible event route each quarter with consenting user feedback funded by the venue; if the developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local mapping vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about later work but secure for the next few years. One paid route is a test of demand, not a retirement business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a venue receive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A measured route from the bus stop to the accessible entrance, with barriers photographed and the user’s feedback noted with consent. I would not call it a legal accessibility certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for mapping work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would test local venues and software employers first. Mae’s restoration customers and our rented home are here, and I am not planning a move.

say: I want **paid route evidence** before AGI reaches mapping code in 2036.
I expect **route robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** without a verified figure.
I can risk **one small project** while preserving ten months of expenses.
do: **Keep testing routes** and save 190 monthly while both wages hold.
**Map paid venue route** quarterly only with employer approval, signed paying client, funded consenting user, costs under 150 and ten-month reserve.
**Seek paid local mapping** after 2036 loss only if vacancies cover rent and bills.
feel: **Uneasy later**, secure in the next few years.
S4.quote: One paid route is a test of demand, not a retirement business.
fieldNote: The **side project** is capped by a signed client, employer permission, funded user feedback and protected reserve.
He calls **future mapping work** conditional, not a guaranteed retirement or wage substitute.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior developer wage could disappear before a safe paid route-survey opening exists. Written notice and a local vacancy that covers rent would help us use the buffer well.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a map is enough to tell a wheelchair user which route works. A photograph cannot tell me how a wheel catches; I need a consenting wheelchair user’s experience to know which route works.

headlineQuote: I need a consenting wheelchair user’s experience to know which route works.
portrait: Colin is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, higher pay and thirteen months saved.
He and Mae **rent** while their grown children live separately.
He **uses AI daily** but checks route maps on foot and with user feedback.
He tests **paid venue mapping** only with a signed client, funded consent, employer permission and ten-month reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his junior wage before safe paid route-survey work appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and a paid local route vacancy covering rent would help.
